new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (4 pp., text, title "Jju phonology", signed "Paul Tench, NBTT, Jos, July 2012"). Page 4, section headed "Tones" (after "Vowels", before the three Hyuwa references) reads exactly: "Tones / Phonology / high ˊ / mid ˗ / low ˋ / Orthography / high ˊ / mid (unmarked) / low ˋ" (modifier letters U+02CA, U+02D7, U+02CB). The quote is verbatim. The whole document is a phoneme/orthography chart (plain, labialized, palatalized, labial-palatalized consonants with fortis series; 7 vowels; 3 tones); the words stress, accent, prominence do not occur anywhere in it, so "tone language, no stress statement" is the correct reading and, since no opened source says anything about word stress, "accessible…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Jju is a register-tone language with three level tones (high, mid, low); the orthography writes high and low with acute and grave accents and leaves mid unmarked. The document contains no statement about word stress at all; no opened source (Tench 2012, McKinney 1984, Oladele 2025, Blench 2018) mentions stress, accent or prominence for Jju.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the chart gives no examples of tone on words.
new_statements.domain_note: Chart-level statement of the tone inventory only; no word- vs phrase-level information. Source is a 4-page phoneme/orthography sheet prepared by a phonologist for the Jju Bible-translation committee, based on Hyuwa's orthography work, not a published grammar.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Jju (Kaje) proper, ISO kaj / jjuu1238, spoken by the Bajju of Zangon Kataf–Kachia area, southern Kaduna State. Blench 2018 (fn. 4, p. 128) notes Jju is usually listed separately from the Tyap cluster (Tyap = kcg, tyap1238) but that the separation 'seems increasingly to reflect ethnic separation rather than linguistic reality'; the Tench 2012 chart follows the Jju Bible-translation orthography (Hyuwa). McKinney 1990/1991 treat Tyap and Jju together but as two languages.

sources.note: Content not seen. It is the original SIL phonemic analysis on which the 1970s orthography (and, via Hyuwa, the H/M/L tone-marking convention) rests; Norton & Harley reproduce its phoneme chart and its discussion of the glottal stop in the negative particle. A 60+-page SIL Nigeria phonology statement of this period normally contains a tone section, but that is an inference, not an observation.
